passage: Vishal, you've told me three times today that you're bad at maths. Who told you that? Listen to your Rajni dadi. When I was eight, our teacher called me "the slow one". Every day: "Rajni, the slow one, try not to hold us up." So I stopped putting my hand up. Why try, if I was slow? My cousin Gopal was "the clever one". He got the hard sums, and he tried them, and he got better. Then in Class 5 a new teacher came. She gave me a hard sum and said, "You can do this. I've seen you think." I sat with it for an hour. I did it. I wasn't slow, beta. I'd just been told so often that I'd started acting it.

qa.q: What did the first teacher call young Rajni?
qa.a: "The slow one."

qa.q: Why did young Rajni stop putting her hand up?
qa.a: Being called slow every day made her believe it, so trying seemed pointless.

qa.q: What might Vishal choose to do the next time a maths problem feels hard?
qa.a: Vishal could sit with it for a while, as young Rajni did in Class 5, instead of deciding in advance to be bad at maths.

qa.q: How might Gopal's schooling have been shaped by being called "the clever one"?
qa.a: Gopal was given hard sums and expected to try them, so he kept getting better, partly because of that label.

grounding: A grandmother recalls how being called slow made her try less while a cousin called clever took on hard work, until a new teacher believed in her.

passage: The inter-class quiz had ten minutes left, the fan was broken, and the hall was so noisy that Naveen and Suraj had to shout to hear each other. Sir dropped the last and hardest question card on their table. "Naveen, you're my clever boy, you take this one. Suraj, try not to be lazy for once, just hold the pen." Naveen grabbed the card and started working, chewing his lip. Suraj slumped back. He'd heard "lazy" so many times this year that he'd stopped doing homework at all. Why bother? "Suraj, what's seven eights?" Naveen hissed. "Fifty-six," Suraj said at once, surprised at himself. "See? You know stuff," Naveen said. Suraj sat up a little, just a little, and picked up the pen properly.

qa.q: What did Sir tell Suraj to do?
qa.a: "Try not to be lazy for once, just hold the pen."

qa.q: Why had Suraj stopped doing homework at all?
qa.a: He felt discouraged after being called lazy so many times, and had started to believe trying was pointless.

qa.q: What did Naveen do that pulled Suraj back in, and what could Sir learn from it?
qa.a: Naveen asked Suraj a real question and said "You know stuff"; Sir could try giving Suraj a real part instead of a label.

qa.q: How might Naveen be affected by always being called the "clever boy"?
qa.a: It makes him grab hard questions confidently, though it may also put pressure on him to always get them right.

grounding: In a noisy, rushed quiz, a child labelled lazy has stopped trying while his friend labelled clever takes on the hardest question.

passage: In the Andheri flat, the twins had names for everything, and so did the grown-ups. Madhav was "our little scientist". Darshan, nine minutes younger, was "the lazy one", said with a laugh at every family dinner. So when the school science fair came, Madhav signed up for the hardest project, a water filter, and worked on it every evening. Darshan said, "I'll just do a poster," and didn't finish that either. "Typical," Papa said. But Kusum maasi, visiting for the week, noticed something: Darshan fixing the broken doorbell with a screwdriver, carefully, for an hour. "That's not lazy," she told him. "That's an engineer." Darshan stared at her. The next evening he asked Madhav if he could help with the filter's pipes.

qa.q: What did Darshan fix with a screwdriver?
qa.a: The broken doorbell.

qa.q: Why might Darshan have said "I'll just do a poster"?
qa.a: After being called the lazy one at every dinner, he may have felt discouraged and believed hard projects weren't meant for him.

qa.q: Which choice by Kusum maasi changed things for Darshan?
qa.a: She noticed his careful work on the doorbell and named it, "That's an engineer", giving him a new label to live up to.

qa.q: How might Madhav's "little scientist" label have shaped his choices?
qa.a: It gave Madhav the confidence to pick the hardest project and keep at it every evening.

grounding: A child called lazy at home gives up on hard tasks while his twin, called a scientist, takes them on, until an aunt sees him differently.

passage:
"Jomon, sums done?"
"No, Ammachi. I'm slow, na. Kishore chettan does them fast."
"Try the first one."
"Why? Everyone says I'm slow. Even Miss."
"Kishore, help your brother."
"Ammachi, I'm doing the Olympiad paper. The hard one. Miss says I'm her clever boy."
"See? He gets the hard ones," Jomon said, and put his pencil down. "I get the easy ones and I still get them wrong."
"Who untangled the whole kite string yesterday? Two hours, all by himself?"
"...Me."
"Slow boys can't do that."
Jomon looked at the first sum for a long time. Then he picked up the pencil again.

qa.q: What was Kishore working on instead of helping?
qa.a: The Olympiad paper, the hard one.

qa.q: Why did Jomon put his pencil down?
qa.a: He believed the 'slow' label everyone used, so trying felt pointless next to his clever brother.

qa.q: What did Ammachi do that helped Jomon pick the pencil up again?
qa.a: She reminded him that he untangled the kite string for two hours by himself, giving him real evidence against the 'slow' label.

qa.q: How has the 'clever boy' label shaped Kishore differently?
qa.a: Being called clever makes Kishore reach for the hard Olympiad paper, while Jomon, called slow, gives up; the labels are steering both boys.

grounding: A boy repeatedly called slow stops trying while his brother, called clever, takes on hard work, until a grandmother points to evidence against the label.

passage: Last year, in Class 5, the dance teacher always called me "Lazy Kavitha", because I came late once. After that, whenever the steps got hard, I thought, why try, I'm the lazy one anyway. I stood at the back and moved slowly. Then, in the new term, Mehak Miss came. On the first day she said, "Kavitha, you have good balance. Can you try the spin at the front?" Nobody had said I had anything good. I practised the spin in our corridor every night. I fell a lot. At the annual day, I did it in the front row. I still think about how one word made me slow, and another made me try.

qa.q: What did the dance teacher call Kavitha?
qa.a: "Lazy Kavitha".

qa.q: How did Kavitha feel whenever the steps got hard?
qa.a: Kavitha felt discouraged and thought, 'why try, I'm the lazy one anyway', because the label had become part of how Kavitha saw things.

qa.q: What choice did Kavitha make after Mehak Miss's words, and what came of it?
qa.a: Kavitha practised the spin in the corridor every night, falling a lot, and finally did it in the front row at the annual day.

qa.q: How might Mehak Miss have seen Kavitha on that first day?
qa.a: Mehak Miss saw good balance, not a lazy child, perhaps because the old label had never reached the new teacher.

grounding: A child labelled lazy starts trying less, and a new teacher's belief leads the child to take on a hard spin.
